summary: Set 129 Session 2 of 2, the final session: A5 is answered, the apparatus is refused, and the note that owned the question has no open items left. A5's answer went into `docs/planning/session-set-authoring-guide.md` beside A1-A4, where an author already looks -- the section is now A1-A5. Three parts: the suite declares its inputs (and derives them from EVIDENCE rather than from the suite's command, which is the trap Session 1 fell into and routed verification caught); the intersection decides the obligation, reported auditably by `run_of_record affected` and consumed once by `evaluate_freshness()`; and modules group and assign ownership without ever selecting suites, because a module axis can only SUBTRACT, would fail open against an unenforced label (L-125-1), and answers nothing a declared input set does not. The corrected safety claim is carried verbatim from `verdict.md` section 2a, with the reason the stronger 'provably redundant work being removed' framing is REFUSED stated in the terms that make it load-bearing: under it a future orchestrator could skip a suite WITHOUT the operator attestation a verification reduction requires, and that reasoning must not be available. The guide also states plainly that A5 authorizes no new skip. Eight refusals with their reasons and six deferrals with their TRIGGER CONDITIONS now sit immediately after A5 as two tables -- a rejection nobody wrote down gets re-proposed by the next reader of a persuasive document, so the refusals are a deliverable rather than a byproduct. A5 is closed in `docs/planning/session-step-skeleton-and-verification-cost.md` with an inline RESOLVED marker that answers its three sub-questions in order, following the note's own convention of preserving the 2026-08-12 diagnosis prose beneath the marker; the note's status header now says no open items remain. `module-organized-projects-recommendation.md` section 6.4 gained the rule that the scope check, when it is built, may never be read as an input to suite selection -- the one place a future author would most plausibly reintroduce the module axis, and the section's own admission that no codeRoots-vs-imports check exists is the argument. Consistency was propagated to every echo in one pass (L-064-8, L-065-1): the guide's 'read covers literally' paragraph, the constitution's Step 8 required-portion sentence, and the suite-key allowlist. Authored `change-log.md` and the router changelog FRAGMENT `ai_router/changelog.d/0110-set-129-suite-owned-input-sets.md` (never an edit to the shared CHANGELOG). The session's one code change was unplanned and test-only, and the TARGETED run found it rather than the verification round: writing this set's own changelog fragment disarmed `test_changelog_round_trip_flags_a_planted_reorder`, which planted its reorder into the two NEWEST fragments while `changelog.check()` deliberately re-renders from the BASELINE set alone -- so the falsifier had only ever fired while at most one post-baseline fragment existed, and a mandatory close-out artifact silently made it two. It now selects from the baseline corpus and asserts that corpus is non-empty (L-112-1), matching the `baseline_fragments()` helper in `test_changelog_partition.py` whose docstring names this exact hazard and which the drift-guard sibling had not used (L-069-1). The gate itself was never wrong. Cross-provider verification: one round, discovery fan-out 2 (spec-conformance, failure-scenario), verifier gpt-5.5 (openai) on both calls, VERIFIED with 0 findings. All three suites were owed -- resolved with the set's own tool rather than by eye, and in every case by the SAME single input, a markdown changelog fragment under `ai_router/` -- and all three ran after the last code change and were recorded fresh and green.
